newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: PNG's Chan says mercenaries to blame for defeat.
newsitem.headline: PNG's Chan says mercenaries to blame for defeat.

text.p: Papua New Guinea's controversial prime minister Sir Julius Chan said on Tuesday his hiring of mercenaries to end a secessionist revolt had contributed to his personal defeat in national elections.
Chan, one of the South Pacific nation's most successful politicians having twice been prime minister, said his 29-year political career was over after he lost his seat in parliament.
"As far as politics is concerned this is probably the end of me," Chan told a news conference in the capital Port Moresby. "After so many years of service to my people, I will re-enter private life."

Chan lost his Namata Nai seat in the New Ireland province to academic Ephraim Apelis on Monday by just 110 votes. Chan had held the seat since Papua New Guinea won independence from Australia in 1975.

In March, Papua New Guinea was plunged into its worst political crisis since independence when the army revolted over Chan's hiring of African mercenaries to end a rebellion on resource-rich Bougainville island.
Chan was forced to temporarily step down pending an inquiry into the US$36 mercenary deal, but was later cleared and returned to office in time for the election.
But a wave of discontent against the Chan government and the mercenary deal has seen a number of ministers lose their seats, including defence minister Mathias Ijape.
Asked by reporters whether his deal with the British military consultancy Sandline International contributed to his defeat, Chan said: "It has a lot to do with it".
"It is a controversial issue, but there were other controversial issues that I had to face as prime minister," he said, referring to big-spending government projects.

"I regret very much that I lost. I had a great dream. I would have liked to have led this country for the next five years and build on the success of the economy that my government was able to achieve," he said.

Chan, 57, is regarded as an astute economic manager who has helped shape his country's transition from a territory reliant solely on aid to an independent nation boasting some of the world's major resource deposits.
Chan said he hoped a member of his People's Progressive Party would become the next prime minister, adding he believed the current political change would be peaceful.
Two weeks of voting closed on Saturday, but because of Papua New Guinea's rugged mountain terrain final results of the election will not be officially declared until July 15.
Chan will step down after offical writs are issued.

Papua New Guinea's splintered party system and the fact that less than one-third of the 2,370 candidates ran on party tickets means the new government will not be automatically formed, but emerge only after political haggling by successful candidates.
The fate of the prime ministership will also be decided through political haggling by parliamentarians.
While Chan's party looks set to win the most seats in the 109-seat parliament, a political opponent looks set to gain the prime ministership.

Political analysts say Michael Somare, the country's first prime minister, looks most likely to become the next prime minister, with his cross-party National Alliance and independents forming the next government. Former prime minister Sir Rabbie Namaliu, speaker in the last parliament, has been re-elected and could pose a threat to Somare.
Only four men have governed Papua New Guinea in the past two decades since independence and two, Chan and Paias Wingti, have both lost their seats in the election.
